cards.title: Occupy the No. 2 position against the leader
cards.summary: If you can't be first in a category, build your brand position by explicitly relating yourself to the leader rather than attacking head-on.
cards.use_when: Choosing positioning for a store or brand entering a category where a dominant competitor already owns the top rung in customer minds (e.g., a new gear shop vs. an established giant).
steps: Identify who owns the mental top spot in your category — the brand customers name first when thinking of the product.
Do not position as a smaller version of the leader or claim you're simply 'better'; that invites a head-on comparison you will lose.
Take the explicit alternative position: state your place relative to the leader (Avis framed itself as 'No. 2' to Hertz rather than trying to out-Hertz Hertz).
Lean into the underdog sympathy that comes with the No. 2 or challenger stance, since customers root for an honest underdog.
Keep the position consistent for years; the source's point is that Avis succeeded because it related itself to Hertz, not because it 'tried harder.'
For an ecommerce store this can mean a PDP/landing-page headline and about-page narrative that names the category leader and defines your brand as the honest alternative.
caveats: The No. 2 strategy requires an actual recognized leader; if the category has no clear leader, the relationship has no anchor.
This is a positioning frame, not proof of sales results — case figures cited come from the source's historical examples, not your market.

cards.title: Find an open 'creneau' inside the prospect's mind, not the factory
cards.summary: Look for an unoccupied position in the customer's mind and claim it first, rather than filling a product gap that only makes sense internally.
cards.use_when: Deciding what new product, size, or category to launch or how to angle a product-page headline for a crowded category.
steps: List the positions already occupied in customers' minds — the established claims competitors own (cheap, premium, large, masculine, morning-use, etc.).

Search for an empty slot customers would recognize, not a gap in your own product line: the source's Volkswagen 'Think small' worked because the small-car position was unclaimed in the mind, even though other small cars existed.
Use reverse thinking: if every competitor is going one direction (bigger, fancier), test the opposite (smaller, simpler).
Test positions along dimensions such as size, price tier, sex/gender coding, age, time of day, distribution channel, or heavy-user usage.
Avoid the Edsel mistake: a hole in the factory lineup (between two models) is not automatically a hole in the customer's mind.
Preempt the position with clear, single-minded messaging on the PDP/landing page — preemption matters more than being merely better.
caveats: The source notes few truly empty positions remain today; many categories require repositioning a competitor instead.
A technical achievement or genuinely new product feature can still fail if no mental slot exists for it (the Frost 8/80 'dry white whisky' example).
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Use price as a positioning claim, stated in advance
cards.summary: High price and low price are each valid positions if you're first to claim them with a credible product story, and the position should be set in your messaging before the customer reaches the store.
cards.use_when: Setting price tier strategy or writing pricing-related copy for a product line or category page.
steps: Decide whether your category rewards a high-price or low-price position: the source argues low-price positions work well for new or unproven products customers are taking a chance on, and high-price positions work for established products with quality or repair concerns.

Claim the tier first: the source says success comes from being first to establish the high-price position with a valid product story in a receptive category (citing examples like Michelob at premium and Mobil 1 synthetic oil).
Communicate the price tier in ads and page copy so there are no price surprises when the customer lands on the product page — price is a feature, stated in advance.
Use the framing, not just a number: 'the costliest,' 'gourmet,' or premium-language headlines position the tier even when exact prices aren't quoted.
Run a portfolio across tiers only if each brand gets its own distinct position and name, as with Budweiser/Michelob/Busch.
caveats: The source explicitly warns that charging high prices is not itself the way to get rich — greed is not positioning.
A high price without a position, product story, and receptive category will drive customers away.
Retailer discount emphasis can erase low-price opportunities over time (the source's generic-brand point).
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Reposition the competitor to create space in the customer's mind
cards.summary: When no open position exists, move an existing competitor out of the mental slot by making the customer change their view of that competitor's product.
cards.use_when: Entering a saturated category where all obvious positions are taken and you need a wedge for your brand story or comparison content.
steps: Find a true, verifiable weakness in the competitor's product or story that customers aren't thinking about (Tylenol used aspirin's stomach irritation and allergy risks).
State the competitor issue first and in detail; Tylenol's ad ran about 60 words on aspirin's downsides before naming its own product.

Make the prospect change their mind about the competitor's product, not just hear praise for yours — Royal Doulton repositioned Lenox as American-made ('Pomona, New Jersey') against its imported-sounding name.
Give the customer a simple, self-verifiable fact, not clever logic; Stolichnaya showed that rival 'Russian' vodkas were actually made in Connecticut, Pennsylvania, and Indiana.

Distinguish repositioning from comparative advertising: 'we're better than X' benchmarks you against the leader and invites 'then why aren't you the leader?' — real repositioning changes the competitor's meaning.
Apply this in comparison pages, ingredient/label content, or category education — e.g., reading the ingredient list aloud as Wise did against Pringle's.
caveats: The source acknowledges repositioning draws ethical complaints, though it argues comparative advertising is legal and can be done honestly and fairly.
Repositioning can backfire if your own product has an unclear name or weak follow-through — Scope's repositioning of Listerine was undercut by an unmouthwash-like name.
Once a product is mentally tagged a loser, the source says recovery is very hard — repositioning works best as an offensive move, not a rescue.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Leader strategy: reinforce the first position instead of repeating 'we're No. 1'
cards.summary: If you own the top position, advertise the product category's value and your original claim rather than boasting about rank.
cards.use_when: Writing brand messaging or category pages when your store genuinely owns the leading mental position in a niche.
steps: Skip 'We're No. 1' copy: either customers know and wonder why you're insecure, or they don't know — which means you defined leadership in your own terms, not theirs.
Reinforce the original concept that got you into the mind first, as Coca-Cola did with 'the real thing' — positioning the brand as the standard others imitate.
Sell the category, not just yourself; the source describes IBM's advertising selling the value of computers generally.
Strengthen with invention claims when true ('we invented the product'), as the source cites for Xerox, Polaroid, and Zippo.
Expand the uses of the product to widen the category — Arm & Hammer promoting baking soda in refrigerators, or orange juice promoted beyond breakfast.
Consider broadening the brand or company name when scope changes, following the Haloid to Xerox pattern.
caveats: Leaders should not read their own ads too admiringly; the source urges covering new developments by adopting promising innovations early or with a multibrand launch.
Ignore-competition messaging assumes genuine category leadership in the customer's mind, not self-declared metrics like 'best-selling above $1,000 east of the Mississippi.'
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Cover competitive moves with a separate brand, not a stretched one
cards.summary: Protect a leading position by launching a distinctly named product for new concepts instead of extending the existing brand into a new meaning.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to launch a new sub-brand, product line, or SKU versus attaching a new variant to your best-selling brand.
steps: Recognize that once a position is established in customers' minds, changing it is very hard; the source points to Procter & Gamble keeping Ivory as a soap and introducing Tide for detergent rather than 'Ivory Detergent.'
Give each genuinely new concept a new name and identity — Cascade rather than 'Dishwasher Tide.'
Follow the pattern of one brand, one position: no Plus, Ultra, or Super add-ons blurring the concept.

Apply the covering principle to new formats or features before a rival claims them: the source cites General Motors buying a Wankel license as cheap insurance, and Kodak/3M declining the xerography rights as the costly opposite.
Budget for the possibility that a new brand cannibalizes some of the old one — the source treats that as preferable to wrecking an established position.
caveats: This is a strategy for brands that already own a strong position; the source warns a follower copying the leader is a 'me-too' move, not covering.
Internal resistance is common — management often sees the new product as a competitor rather than protection, so the covering move is hard to sell internally.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Don't fall into the F.W.M.T.S. trap
cards.summary: After a successful positioning campaign, keep the same position for years instead of drifting into aspiration or new campaigns that abandon what worked.
cards.use_when: Reviewing brand messaging, campaign themes, or homepage copy that has accumulated multiple taglines over time.
steps: Audit how many different themes your brand has run; the source notes that despite Avis's many campaigns, the one theme people remember is the original 'No. 2' idea.
Identify the single concept you actually own in the customer's mind and make it the consistent spine of your messaging.
Don't advertise aspirations that contradict your position (Avis's 'Avis is going to be No. 1' abandoned the underdog sympathy and No. 2 relationship that was working).
Reuse the same position across campaigns, product pages, and ads rather than rotating fresh taglines for novelty.
Accept that a strong position may cap some ambitions — if you can't exploit a real leader weakness, the source says you're not destined to be No. 1 just by wishing it.
caveats: The source treats consistency as the core positioning discipline; it doesn't argue you can never launch new products, only that the owned position shouldn't be abandoned.
Failing to hold your position risks being passed by a competitor, as the source warns about Avis and National.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Check whether you can even 'get there from here'
cards.summary: Before pouring budget into a category push, honestly assess whether your current position makes the goal achievable at all, since effort cannot overcome a structurally hopeless position.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to enter a new product category, compete with a dominant platform, or fund an aggressive growth goal.
steps: Identify the entrenched leader and its share (the source cites IBM's 70% of the mainframe business): head-on attacks against a mental leader have no hope of progress.
Do not mimic the leader's approach — acting like IBM in the source's example is the most common and fatal mistake of bigger challengers.

Instead, relate your existing owned position to the new category: the source suggested RCA (a communications leader) should position computers around communications, and GE around its time-sharing strength; NCR progressed by focusing on retail data-entry (computerized cash registers).
Where the situation is genuinely hopeless, redirect resources to areas of your business where you do hold a position; the source argues outright failure is often preferable to mediocre success.
Distinguish strategic positions where extra effort early builds leadership from ones where no amount of money or can-do spirit closes the gap.
caveats: The RCA and GE computer outcomes are historical case examples, not predictions about your market; treat them as illustrations of a rule about head-on competition.
The source also says extra effort is valuable when applied early to establish leadership — timing matters, so 'can't get there' applies mainly to late, head-on moves.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Avoid the everybody trap and commit to a specific niche
cards.summary: In a crowded market, appeal to everyone dilutes your position; carve out a specific slot even if you lose some customers doing so.
cards.use_when: Writing category, homepage, or brand copy and choosing whether to keep broad, inclusive messaging or commit to a defined customer segment.
steps: Accept that being all things to all people can keep an established brand afloat but is deadly when building a position from nothing.
Choose a specific position along a real dimension (use case, price tier, customer segment, ingredient stance) and state it unambiguously, as Volkswagen did with 'Think small.'
Accept that taking a strong position makes some enemies or excludes some buyers — the source argues you can't win by stepping on no one's toes.
Avoid multiple vague value claims competing for space on the same page; one clear position beats a list of universal benefits.
Recognize the volume of competing messages customers face — the source compares sorting product names to a vocabulary problem, so a single claim is what can register.
caveats: This is the source's advice for brands trying to build a position; it concedes a broad, already-dominant brand may survive without a sharp niche.
The source's argument rests on the overcommunicated-market premise, not on measured conversion data.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Make the product name do positioning work
cards.summary: The name is the hook that hangs a brand on the ladder in the customer's mind, and the source calls it the single most important marketing decision.
cards.use_when: Naming a new product, private label, or sub-brand, or diagnosing why a well-positioned offer underperforms.
steps: Choose a name that supports the intended position rather than contradicting it — the source argues Scope's repositioning of Listerine was partly undone because 'Scope' sounds like a board game, not a good-tasting mouthwash.
Avoid house-name extensions for genuinely new concepts, since they trade a quick share of market for a diluted position.
Prefer names that reinforce the positioning angle, such as Luke's masculine name or 'Old Milwaukee' for a low-priced beer versus the owner's own name on the cheapest brand.

Remember the source's claim about sensory expectations: people 'taste what they expect to taste,' so a name and copy implying artificiality can make the product itself seem worse (the Pringle's ingredient-list backlash).
Test the name against the mind's existing associations, not just internal brand logic.
caveats: The naming failures cited (Scope, Max Factor's 'Just Call Me Maxi') are historical anecdotes presented as illustrations, not controlled evidence.
The source treats the name as critical but does not claim a name alone fixes a product with no position.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Race on launch speed and budget, not late 'better'
cards.summary: Most me-too products fail because they spend time improving the product while a competitor establishes leadership first; speed, launch budget, and a good name beat incremental superiority.
cards.use_when: Planning a product or category launch, deciding launch timing, naming, and marketing spend against an incumbent.
steps: Prioritize being first to establish the position over making a marginally better version; the source says accent should be on speed, not 'better.'
Give the launch a substantial budget — the source warns the opposite happens: me-too brands waste time, then launch with a smaller budget than the leader's.
Give the new product its own name rather than the house name, since house names are the easy way to get quick share but a positioning trap.
If you're late and can't be first, use a follower strategy (alternative position or repositioning the leader) rather than a better-me-too claim.
Weigh timing explicitly, as the source does when describing Lorillard's late masculine cigarette brand 'Luke' failing about 20 years after Marlboro claimed masculinity.
caveats: The source's claim about 'first gets twice the long-term share' is presented as a general historical pattern, not a formula or a guaranteed benchmark for your category.
This reflects the source's view that first-mover advantage dominates; a truly differentiated late entry can still win, but not by fighting the leader head-on.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Turn sensory expectation into a merchandising and copy lever
cards.summary: Customers taste and judge what they expect to taste, so ingredient and description language on the page shapes perceived product quality.
cards.use_when: Writing product page copy, ingredient lists, or label descriptions for food, supplements, or any product judged by sensory quality.
steps: Recognize that consumer taste is partly mental: the source notes Pringle's common complaint was 'tastes like cardboard' after rivals read its industrial-sounding ingredient list on TV.
Keep ingredient and process copy human and concrete; long chemical names invite negative perception even when the product is fine.
Use the water-vs-'dihydrogen oxide' example as the principle: identical substances can be perceived differently based on the words used.
When a competitor's formulation is technically fine but sounds unappealing, you can reposition it honestly by focusing attention on what it contains, as Borden's Wise did comparing ingredient lists.
Pair sensory-expectation copy with the actual product experience so expectations don't outrun reality.
caveats: The Pringle's outcome is a historical case, not a controlled test; use as illustration, not a guaranteed result.
Once a product is widely perceived as a 'loser,' the source says recovering is very hard, so this lever works better ahead of negative perception than after.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Competitive ads vs. repositioning ads: know the difference
cards.summary: Most comparative advertising fails because it benchmarks against the leader instead of changing the customer's view of that leader's product.
cards.use_when: Planning comparison content, 'us vs. them' pages, or competitor-focused acquisition creative.
steps: Avoid the 'we're better than X, Y, Z' structure; the prospect reacts with 'then why aren't you the leader?', and you're saying what they already expect you to say.

Instead, state something about the competitor's product that changes the customer's understanding: Tylenol on aspirin's risks, Royal Doulton on Lenox's American origin, Stolichnaya on rivals' US production.
Run the competitor-framing portion first and in real detail before mentioning your own product — the source notes Tylenol's roughly 60 words of aspirin copy before naming itself.
Be factually accurate to keep the tactic honest and defensible; the source cites these as verifiable claims, not invented ones.

Keep in mind that such claims are legally permitted in many markets (the source traces US TV comparative-ad acceptance to FTC pressure in the 1970s), but verify current rules and platform policies for your market.
caveats: Repositioning draws ethical objections, which the source acknowledges while defending it as more effective than brag-and-boast.
Comparative claims carry legal and platform risk; the source's regulatory timeline is historical and specific rules should be verified with counsel.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Treat equality between top brands as unstable
cards.summary: When two brands run neck and neck, the category is unstable and one will usually pull ahead; that's when extra effort pays off most.
cards.use_when: Timing a promotional push or brand investment in a category where you're roughly tied with a rival for the top spot.
steps: Watch for a genuine dead heat at the top of a category — the source argues it's inherently unstable and typically resolves to a lasting lead (citing Hertz/Avis, Harvard/Yale, and the Ford/Chevrolet race resolved by Chevrolet in 1931).
Concentrate extra marketing effort during that period of doubt rather than spreading it evenly, since the source says the time for extra effort is when neither side has clear superiority.
Expect a near-term win to lock in a long-term advantage; the source says winning sales leadership in a single year often clinches victory for decades.

Recognize leader advantages beyond sales — preferential retail stocking, better hiring, and customer default repurchase habits (buying the same brand as last time) — and account for them in your plan.
Once ahead, shift from fight to defense: use short-term flexibility to protect the long-term position rather than continuing to spend as if tied.
caveats: These patterns come from historical consumer-goods and auto examples; the source presents them as general positioning rules, not modern measured benchmarks.
The 'twice the long-term share' figure is a source heuristics claim, not a calculation to plan against literally.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Position by a category dimension before rivals do
cards.summary: Sex, age, time of day, distribution channel, and usage intensity are all positionable dimensions — first to claim them wins, latecomers fail.
cards.use_when: Choosing an angle for a new product, line, or landing-page narrative in a mature category where broad claims are taken.
steps: Survey the category for unclaimed dimensions: gender coding (Marlboro's masculinity, Virginia Slims' femininity), age (Geritol for older customers, Aim toothpaste for children), time of day (Nyquil as the first night-time cold remedy), distribution (L'eggs in supermarkets), and heavy-user framing (Schaefer for the frequent beer drinker).
Pick a dimension you can be first to own; the source emphasizes timing is critical and cites late me-toos like Eve and Luke as failures against earlier claimants.
Consider the counterintuitive direction: the source notes the largest perfume became Charlie, the first brand to use a masculine name with pantsuit advertising, even though most brands were feminine.
If a rival already owns the dimension, don't copy it — a me-too naming and ad campaign on the same axis tends to fail.
Translate the chosen dimension into a specific, single-minded claim in the product page headline and imagery.
caveats: Numeric share claims like Aim's '10 percent of the toothpaste market' are historical examples, not targets.
The source's timing claims are anecdotal case comparisons, not controlled tests, so validate demand for the dimension with customers before building around it.
